newsitem.title: USA: Dollar hits lowest level in more than four months vs yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits lowest level in more than four months vs yen.

text.p: NEW YORK, May 15 - The dollar plunged against the Japanese yen on Thursday to its weakest level in more than four months on expectations that Japan will raise interest rates.
But the dollar rose against the German mark amid concern that the German government may revalue some of its gold to help shrink the country's yawning budget deficit.

In Europe, the dollar plummetted to 114.70 yen, its lowest level since Dec. 27. The U.S. currency has fallen 10 percent against the yen since soaring to a four-and-a-half-year high of 127.45 yen on May 1.
Growing speculation that record low official Japanese interest rates could rise stemmed partly from remarks made by a senior Japanese legislator on Thursday.

Jiji news agency quoted Koichi Kato, secretary-general of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, as saying Japan may face pressure to change its current low interest rates as it progresses with financial market deregulation.
The Bank of Japan has kept its rates at rock-bottom levels to bolster economic growth.

Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer & Co. in New York, cited "the outlook for Japanese rates and people unwinding the positions that they've had on for a couple of years now" as reasons for the dollar's sharp decline.
"Soon as we got under the 115 level, there was some short covering interest and it took us right back up to 116," Strauss added.

The dollar, however, seesawed on either side of 116 yen during New York trading. Some traders felt remarks by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin late in the day provided mild support to the embattled currency.
Rubin repeated his support for a strong dollar and said a strong dollar boosts market confidence, cuts interest rates and keeps inflation low.

Asked if Rubin's remarks aided the dollar, Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank, said, "I think so. I think they are getting to a point -- Rubin and also the Japanese officials -- where they think dollar-yen's fallen far enough in the short run."
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 115.97 yen, down from 117.23 yen late Wednesday. But the dollar rose to 1.6980 marks from 1.6947 marks.

Tax experts revealed on Thursday that Germany faces an estimated 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) shortfall in tax revenues this year, which might hurt German efforts to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union or EMU.
Separately, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a news conference on Thursday that the Bundesbank's gold reserves should be revalued at close to the market level.
A revaluation of the gold held at the central bank would provide windfall profits of about 40 billion marks ($23.6 billion) based on current market prices.

Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc., said the dollar was supported by a surprisingly big rise in core consumer prices in April, which raised the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again next Tuesday.
The Labour Department said the Consumer Price Index rose a mere 0.1 percent in April. But the index gained 0.3 percent in the core rate, which excludes volatile food and energy items.
The dollar fell to 1.4305 Swiss francs from 1.4364 francs, and to Canadian $1.3713 from C$1.3901.
The British pound slid to $1.6427 from $1.6470.
